summary: Proposes adding Kerberos-based cipher suites to TLS, so that a TLS connection can authenticate using Kerberos. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: TLS usually checks ID cards called certificates. This lets it check Kerberos tickets instead, like a concert wristband.

subtitle: Lets a TLS connection authenticate with Kerberos tickets instead of public-key certificates.

tldr.problem: TLS authentication was limited to public key solutions, so it did not fit organizations that rely on symmetric-key authentication systems such as Kerberos.
tldr.mechanism: New cipher suites select Kerberos. The client sends a Kerberos ticket, an optional authenticator and a pre-master secret encrypted under the Kerberos session key inside the ClientKeyExchange message.
tldr.outcome: The handshake gains a master secret and mutual authentication without any new messages. The 40-bit suites are listed only to document assigned codes and are strongly discouraged.

today: RFC 2712 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its IESG note strongly discourages the 40-bit cipher suites it documents.

sections.title: Kerberos Meets TLS
sections.content:
TLS lets clients and servers negotiate cipher suites to match their security and administrative policies. Until this RFC, though, authentication in TLS was limited to public key solutions, so organizations with authentication systems based on symmetric cryptography were not fully served.

Kerberos, which the RFC calls the most widely deployed symmetric key authentication system, is described in RFC 1510. This document adds a Kerberos option to the TLS framework (RFC 2246). The RFC calls the change minimal, no different from adding a new public key algorithm.
sections.eli5: Some places check ID cards and others use tickets. This lets the secure-connection system work with places that use tickets too.

sections.title: New Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The TLS security context is chosen in the client and server hello messages. The RFC defines new cipher suites whose names start with TLS_KRB5. They use DES, 3DES, RC4 with 128 bits, or IDEA for the bulk cipher, and SHA or MD5 for the MAC. Their codes run from 0x00,0x1E through 0x00,0x25. Six more export suites, with 40-bit keys, take codes 0x00,0x26 through 0x00,0x2B.

To use Kerberos, the client lists one or more of these suites in its client hello. A server that supports the option confirms the chosen Kerberos suite in its server hello.

An IESG note says the 40-bit suites are included only to document that their codes were already assigned. They were designed for now-obsolete export restrictions, were never secure, and implementing or using them is strongly discouraged.
sections.eli5: The client shows a menu of secret-code styles, and the server picks one. This RFC adds new menu items that use Kerberos tickets.

sections.title: The Kerberos ClientKeyExchange
sections.content:
The ClientKeyExchange message gets a new case. When the key exchange algorithm is krb5, the message carries a KerberosWrapper instead of an RSA-encrypted or Diffie-Hellman value.

The wrapper holds three parts: the Kerberos Ticket, an optional authenticator, and the EncryptedPreMasterSecret, encrypted with the session key sealed in the ticket. The ticket and authenticator are encoded per RFC 1510 (ASN.1 encoding).
sections.eli5: The client hands over a sealed envelope with its ticket and a secret note that only the ticket's owner and the server can open.

sections.title: How the Handshake Changes
sections.content:
To use this option, the client must first obtain a service ticket for the TLS server. In TLS, the ClientKeyExchange passes a random 48-byte pre-master secret to the server. Both sides then derive the master secret from it independently, and use that for session keys and MAC computations. With Kerberos the pre-master secret has the same structure as in the RSA case, but it is encrypted under the Kerberos session key. The server uses its secret key to unwrap the credentials and extract the pre-master secret.

Several optional TLS messages are left out: the server's Certificate, the ServerKeyExchange, the CertificateRequest and the client's Certificate. Authentication and the master secret come from the client's Kerberos credentials, and TLS already marks those messages optional. The authenticator is not required, because the master secret is seeded with a random value from the server hello, which foils replay attacks. It remains optional because it can carry authorization information.

After the Finished messages are exchanged, the master secret is established and mutual authentication is achieved, because the server proves it knows the master secret in its Finished message. No new messages are added.
sections.eli5: The client and server both use the ticket to agree on a shared secret. The server proves it knows the secret, so each side knows who the other is.

sections.title: Naming the Server
sections.content: To get the right service ticket, the client must know the Kerberos principal name of the TLS server. The RFC uses the form host/MachineName@Realm. The literal host follows the Kerberos convention when the protection domain on a machine does not matter, MachineName is the particular instance of the service, and Realm is the domain name of the machine.
sections.eli5: To get the right ticket, the client has to spell the server's name in the exact way Kerberos expects.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Kerberos cipher suites are subject to the same security considerations as TLS. Just as a public key implementation must protect its private key, a Kerberos implementation must protect the long lived secret shared between the principal and the KDC. A weak password may be open to a dictionary attack.

To strengthen the first authentication to the KDC, an implementor may use secondary authentication with a token card, or initial authentication based on public key cryptography, commonly known as PKINIT.
sections.eli5: A ticket system is only as safe as the secret behind it. A guessable password is like a lock that opens with the first key you try.
